reason: Banner petal 'present' only makes sense when the banner itself is absent or present. Most examples are about a callus, spur, auricles or appendages on the banner, and those belong to the sub-part. A rule would need to send 'without/with X' to X and keep 'present' for the petal only.

'Plant organ base' is a generic part with no organ, and the examples are all 'style base'. The bearer should be style, with the base as a position. Same treatment as the other generic parts rejected on 2026-11-13.

'Single' means one (solitary) in most examples ('lower ones single', 'single in a bract sheath'), not 'simple' (unbranched). A spike can be simple, but a rule must separate count 'single' from 'unbranched'.
A floral disc can be oblong, but the examples describe disc lobes and calli. A rule would need to assign the shape to the lobe or callus when one is named.
Furrowed abaxial surface of the lamina is meaningful and the examples fit.
Disc length compared with the ovary or flowers is meaningful, and the examples are annotated correctly.
The orchid epichile is often recurved.

The examples mostly describe calyx teeth or lobes, with some for the whole calyx. A rule would need to assign the shape to the calyx lobe when 'teeth' is named. The whole calyx is not triangular-lanceolate.
Wrong reading: 'compressed' here means flattened (dorsiventrally, vertically), not condensed. It needs a flattened or compressed shape term.
Winged keels are normal, in the legume keel petal and in keeled structures generally.
A fleshy orchid column is a normal character.
Cycad megasporophylls are tomentose, and the examples are correct.
A moss costa can be flat or broad and flat.
A strobilus can be sessile or stalked.
'Persistent' protonema maps to non-deciduous, and the examples fit.
Length of a vaginant lamina, including relative length such as 'half the length of the leaf', is meaningful.
Tessellated (chequered) petals occur, for example in Fritillaria. There is only one flora.
A mericarp bearing glandular trichomes is glandular. The examples say so directly.
Tapering stamens, filament or apex, is meaningful.
A truncate labellum apex or base is meaningful, and the examples fit.
Hispidulous stipules are normal.
Clavate vittae are a standard character in Apiaceae fruit descriptions.
Wrong bearer: 'seeds per legume' counts the seeds, and 'legume 1 per umbel' is a count of another unit. The count belongs to the counted part (seed) under the counted-parts rule.
Pyramidal panicles are standard.
An acuminate labellum or epichile apex is meaningful.
Relative size of labellum lobes (larger, subequal) is meaningful.
Terminal seta (position at the tip) is meaningful.
Presence or absence of phyllopodia is the character in the examples.
Bifid or furcate leaf lobes are meaningful.
A decurrent ligule base on both sides is meaningful, and the examples fit.
Spotted achenes are normal.
'Structure' is too generic. The examples say 'proliferous bulbil', which means the bulbil sprouts and is not a structure value. It needs a specific term or the bulbil presence pattern.
Colour of the leaf midvein, such as straw-coloured, is meaningful.
Indumentum can be monomorphic or dimorphic, which is a morphology character. The attribute is generic.
Indumentum density is meaningful.
Rudimentary carpels in male flowers are vestigial.
'Divided for 1/3-1/2' may refer to anther lobes or the connective appendage rather than a dissected anther. A rule would need the sub-part (lobe, theca, appendage) named.
Keeled stems or internodes are meaningful. Some French examples say 'côtelée' (ribbed), a different character.
The examples (fibrils and pores, a single pore) look like cell-wall features of hyaline cells, not the stem. Wrong part, and 'a single pore' is a count.
Clustered pedicels are meaningful.

'Numerous', 'only at margin' and 'sparse' describe amount and position of the glands, not presence. A rule would need to send those to amount or position and keep 'present' for explicit presence or absence.
An auriculate labellum or lobe is meaningful.
Pale anthers are a colour intensity. Where a hue is named ('vert pâle'), the hue term should also be taken.
Wrong reading: 'irregular flower' means irregular (zygomorphic) symmetry, not an irregular spatial pattern. It needs the symmetry term.
An attenuate capsule base or apex is meaningful.
The examples describe hyaline cells, cell surface or leaf base corrugations, so the bearer is not the whole leaf. A rule would need to assign them to cell or surface.
Capitulum size is meaningful.
Disc glands can be turbinate, obovoid or conical.
Whole-plant tolerance (drought, salt) is meaningful. The stressor must stay in the statement.
A fringed stigma is meaningful.
A boat-shaped (naviculaire) receptacle is meaningful, though 'cymbiformes' may refer to scales on it.
A small cotyledon is meaningful.
Woody ('ligneuse') capsules are meaningful.
Papery ('papyracée') legume walls are meaningful.

The examples mix fruit orientation ('dressées ou pendantes'), inclusion in the calyx, and hair orientation ('poils étalés'). A rule would need to keep only the fruit's own position and send hair statements to the hair.
Glandular legumes (glandular hairs on the surface) are meaningful.

'À glandes' states that glands are present on the androgynophore, and the glands are a part with their own number and shape. A rule would need to send those to the gland and keep 'glandular' for a glandular surface.
Tomentose drupes are meaningful.
Glossy or shiny legumes are meaningful.
Wrong bearer: the depth or thickness belongs to a mat, water or a layer, not the whole plant.
